column3: It repeats the focus formula exactly while adding the assurance that no soul is wronged.

It applies the same deed-for-deed recompense to the futility of excuses on that day.
It begins the immediate surah scene by gathering the wrongdoers for the outcome stated in the focus.

It directly continues the focus context by showing the condemned sharing punishment.
It introduces the same surah's relation between God, human beings, and what they do.

It continues the immediate movement of the wrongdoers toward Hell.

It joins return to God with disclosure of what people used to do.

It ties humiliating punishment to false speech about God and arrogance toward His signs.
It repeats the surah's reward refrain without adding to the earlier instance.

The great triumph is a broad result image without an explicit deed-recompense link.
It repeats the formula within a leader-follower scene of regret and shared culpability.

It names the event in the immediate context as the Day of Recompense.
It repeats the exclusive recompense formula while distinguishing the return for good and evil deeds.
It is another instance of the already established surah refrain about rewarding good-doers.
It combines erasure of worst deeds with reward according to the best of them.
It repeats the same reward refrain without a new contribution.
The warning about concealed hostility does not materially address recompense for deeds.
The truthfulness of the messenger does not directly develop the focus's judgment statement.

Turning away for a time does not clarify the focus's relation of deeds and return.

It repeats the earlier command to turn away without adding a recompense connection.
It presents lasting paradise as a reward corresponding to what its people did.

The reciprocal command to act is only a distant counterpart to accountability for actions.
The statement about inability to tempt does not clarify recompense for deeds.

It combines removal of evil deeds with reward according to the best of righteous works.

The command to act justly and remember divine instruction is only indirectly related to later recompense.
Abraham's disavowal after learning the truth does not develop deed-based recompense.

It joins the gathering before God with every soul receiving in full what it earned and no injustice.

It makes full payment for deeds on the Day of Resurrection explicit.
It supplies the divine justice principle that God does not wrong even an atom's weight and multiplies good.
It specifies the proportional contrast of multiplied good and unwronged repayment for evil.
It assigns degrees according to what people did and denies that God is unaware of their deeds.
It explicitly says the Lord will pay every person in full for their deeds.
It depicts each soul pleading for itself and being paid in full for what it did without injustice.
It attaches each person's deed to them and presents it as an opened record on the Day of Resurrection.
It calls the person to read their own record, making personal accounting explicit.
It presents the record with every deed found present and declares that the Lord wrongs no one.
It states the concealed Hour will come so that every soul may be recompensed for its striving.
It establishes just scales for the Day of Resurrection, with no soul wronged even by a mustard seed.
It links heavy scales directly to successful outcomes on that day.
It records what people sent ahead and their traces, supplying an accounting basis for recompense.
It states that every soul will be paid in full for what it did while God fully knows their acts.
It declares that each soul is recompensed for what it earned and that there is no injustice that day.
It contrasts an evil deed's like-for-like return with believers' entry into paradise and unmeasured provision.
It states that God created in truth so every soul may be recompensed for what it earned without injustice.
It states that God recompenses those who do evil for what they did and rewards those who do good.
It limits a human being to what they strive for, directly grounding the focus's link between deeds and return.
It says each person's striving will be seen, providing the disclosure preceding recompense.
It states that the striving will then receive the fullest recompense.
It makes every soul answerable for what it earned.
It says the human being will be informed of what they sent ahead and left behind.
It explicitly characterizes the punishment as a fitting recompense.
It establishes appointed guardians over people before the following disclosure that they know what people do.
It specifies those recorders as noble scribes.
It states that the scribes know what people do, grounding subsequent judgment.
It gives the person who receives their record in the right hand a direct accounting scene.
It states that such a person will receive an easy reckoning.
It gives the contrasting case of receiving one's record from behind the back.
It states that whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it.
It states that whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it.
It states that every soul will be paid in full for what it earned and that none will be wronged.
It assigns each soul the good it earned and the evil it acquired, sharpening personal responsibility.
It makes the weighing on that day true and links heavy scales to success.
It gives the contrasting loss of those whose scales are light because they wronged God's signs.
It says every soul will be tested for what it sent ahead and returned to its true Master.
It says those seeking worldly life are paid in full for their deeds there, without diminution.
It explicitly states that God recompenses every soul for what it earned.
It promises believers who act righteously a good life and reward by the best of what they did.
It makes hearing, sight, and heart each subject to questioning, extending personal accountability.
It states that God does not let the reward of those who do good works be lost.
It affirms that the effort of a believing righteous worker is not denied and is recorded.
It depicts deeds found void at final encounter, where God gives the account in full.
It promises believers who do righteous deeds an abiding reward according to their work.
It directly joins tasting enduring punishment to forgetting the meeting of that day and what people used to do.
It gives believers who do righteous deeds forgiveness and generous provision as their recompense.
It states that God gives workers their rewards in full and increases them from bounty.
It promises the patient their reward without measure, adding a distinct mode of recompense.
It contrasts increased harvest for one who seeks the Hereafter with limited worldly harvest for another.
It relates affliction to what hands have earned while also naming divine pardon.
It assigns degrees according to deeds so each may be paid in full for what they did without injustice.
It makes every person held in pledge for what they earned, alongside the joining of believing descendants.
It gives the Day of Gathering as the setting where God removes evil deeds and admits believers to gardens.
It links belief and righteous action to entry into gardens beneath which rivers flow.
Receiving the record in the right hand supplies a concrete outcome of the completed accounting.
It directly identifies the described bliss as a reward and the recipients' effort as appreciated.
It announces that the defrauders will be raised for a tremendous day, situating their deeds before judgment.
It makes heavy scales the determinant of a satisfying life.
It gives light scales as the contrasting determinant of ruin.
